analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-based public health plan anyone could buy, and lets Medicare negotiate drug prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created 'Medicare Part E' plans — government-run health plans sold on the insurance exchanges and offered voluntarily to employers — with gold-level coverage, including abortion and reproductive care that states could not block. It would also let Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices for the first time, cap seniors' out-of-pocket costs at $6,700 a year, and make ACA tax credits larger, reach higher incomes, and buy more generous plans. It also included $10 billion in reinsurance to stabilize the individual insurance market.
analysis.who_benefits: Any U.S. resident not already on Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP could buy a public plan with gold-level coverage on the exchanges, through an employer, or by keeping it after losing a job. People buying their own coverage would get bigger tax credits available up to 600% of the poverty line, benchmarked to more generous gold plans, plus deeper cost-sharing help. Medicare enrollees would gain a $6,700 annual out-of-pocket cap, and everyone with Medicare drug coverage would benefit from government-negotiated prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured consumers, plus Medicare enrollees

how_it_helps.text: Creates Medicare Part E public plans available in the individual, small-group, and large-group markets, with gold-level benefits and coverage of abortion and reproductive services that state laws cannot block.

Repeals the Medicare 'noninterference' rule and requires the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate Part D drug prices, with a fallback to the lower of the VA or federal procurement price if talks fail after a year.
Caps Medicare beneficiaries' annual out-of-pocket cost-sharing at $6,700 starting in 2020, indexed to medical inflation.
Expands ACA premium tax credits to households up to 600% of the poverty line, switches the benchmark to the second-lowest-cost gold plan, and deepens cost-sharing reductions for low-income enrollees.
Appropriates $10 billion for a three-year state reinsurance program to lower premiums in the individual market, and extends community-rating rules to large employer plans.
Requires employers that offer unaffordable or bare-bones plans to refer full-time workers to exchange navigators, and funds navigator capacity.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would face a government-backed competitor with Medicare-scale administrative costs. Brand-name drug makers would face government price negotiation for the first time. Hospitals and providers would be paid rates capped between Medicare levels and commercial exchange averages. Taxpayers would fund a $2 billion startup appropriation, initial reserves, the $10 billion reinsurance program, and expanded tax credits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, drug makers, providers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Part E plans would pay providers at rates no higher than exchange averages and no lower than Medicare rates in the aggregate; providers argued this could shift costs or narrow networks, and the bill automatically deems every existing Medicare provider a participant, which critics saw as coercive.
The $10 billion reinsurance program subsidizes insurance companies' risk, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge as industry stabilization purchased with federal money.

The bill appropriates $2 billion in startup funding plus expanded tax credits and mandatory cost-sharing support with no offset, adding to federal spending; the credit expansion to 600% of poverty is a large, uncapped entitlement increase.

The nationwide abortion-coverage mandate with federal funding, and the explicit override of state and federal funding restrictions, would have drawn certain defeat on values grounds in a Republican Senate even if the rest of the bill had advanced.
Voluntary employer plans could let some employers drop existing coverage over time, relying on the public plan as a fallback, though the bill only offers participation, not a mandate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-side benefits are large and concrete: a cheaper public option, bigger and broader tax credits, an out-of-pocket cap for seniors, and government drug negotiation. The main costs are federal spending with no identified offset, the $10 billion that flows to insurers as reinsurance, and real adjustment risk for providers who would see payment rates pulled toward Medicare levels. The package is a serious attempt to broaden coverage and cut prices, though its financing is thin and the provider-rate design would have been contested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on April 18, 2018, joined by 14 Democratic cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance that same day; no further action was ever taken on it.
The Finance Committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and it never received a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

All 15 sponsors were Democrats, and the bill text shows the scale of what was set aside: a public plan option, Medicare drug price negotiation, a $6,700 Medicare out-of-pocket cap, expanded tax credits to 600% of poverty, and a $10 billion reinsurance program.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and brand-name drug makers kept the status quo: no public competitor on the exchanges and no government price negotiation for Medicare drugs. Consumers who would have gained cheaper plans and lower drug prices got none of it.

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Choose Medicare Act and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 14 of 47 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of them sat on the majority side of the chamber, and none chaired the committee it went to.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee on April 18, 2018, and the committee took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; with Republicans holding the Senate majority and the Finance chair, the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: A Medicare-based public plan sold on the same exchanges would compete directly with private plans, backed by lower administrative costs and rates capped below commercial averages. Insurers' interest in blocking it ran against consumers seeking cheaper coverage.

The bill repeals the statutory ban on Medicare drug price negotiation and directs HHS to negotiate, with a VA-price fallback for drugs where talks fail. Manufacturers' pricing power was the bill's direct target.

Part E rates are capped between Medicare and commercial exchange averages, cutting payments compared to private insurance, but every Medicare provider is automatically a participating provider, guaranteeing patient volume. Patients would pay less; providers would be paid less.

industries.industry: Insurance brokers, navigators, and exchange infrastructure
industries.note: The bill funds navigator grants and requires employers to refer workers to navigators, expanding demand for enrollment assistance.
